pass_a_gloss: one another, will think it said as equivalent to forgiving one another, especially because of as God in Christ forgave us, and will bring these things upon remission of sins, saying we must forgive those who sin against us as God also forgave us our sins. How then did God in Christ forgive us our sins? Or because the Father, being in Christ, forgave us the trespasses? And in Christ he also granted us the good things, if indeed in Christ there is wisdom which he granted us, and truth and righteousness. But fornication and all uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints, and shamefulness and foolish talk or coarse jesting, which are not proper, but rather thanksgiving. Origen says: fellowship with a harlot according to Scripture's custom is named fornication; but every sin according to the place of fleshly ticklings, not only according to adulteries and corruptions of children but also according to the other things human licentiousness invented in various and manifold frictions, is named uncleanness as a genus. Greed one must take either more simply, or, as we showed elsewhere, adultery, when we also used "not to go beyond and defraud each his brother." And all uncleanness must be guarded against, since this is fitting for saints. There is a certain shamefulness according to each kind of licentiousness; and shamefulness is similar to uncleanness; for each act according to the place of the activity toward secretion shows both the unclean and the shameful; and these things must be said of what is against nature, not of marriage. Let us also see what foolish talk is, which itself must not even be named among the saints. Someone will say, taking the wording more simply, that foolish talk is what buffoons and laugh-makers practice. But see whether those alienated from any wisdom and understanding whatever must also be said to talk foolishly, and foolish in the things they dogmatize. And coarse jesting attached to it will seem to agree with taking foolish talk more simply—custom of the unlearned ranks it upon those who move laughter not only from foolish talk but from any cause whatever. Neither is this proper for the saints, but rather thanksgiving toward God in all things, or thanksgiving according to which we call some gracious and charming. So one must not be a foolish-talker and coarse jester, but gracious and charming; and since it is unusual to say but rather graciousness, perhaps instead of that he used the word lying upon another and said but rather thanksgiving. And perhaps it is custom for those from the Hebrews to use the name thanksgiving and the thankful instead of graciousness and the gracious; such we thought also the saying in Proverbs a gracious woman raises glory for a husband instead of a charming woman; and we would have seemed to force gracious woman taken as charming, if the other editions did not agree with this reading. For Aquila rendered a woman of grace holds to glory, and Theodotion and Symmachus a woman of grace will hold to glory. For this you know, that every fornicator or unclean person or greedy person, who is an idolater, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. One must observe that forbidding six sins—fornication and uncleanness and greed and shamefulness and foolish talk and coarse jesting—he does not bring upon the six so that the one held by any of them has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, but three, I mean fornication and all uncleanness and greed. For if the one liable to foolish talk and coarse jesting also had no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God, the judgment that forgives our weak nature in nothing would seem harsher to someone. For otherwise these too are not proper, yet not so that when they are practiced someone falls from the inheritance of Christ and God. It remains also to attend about shamefulness. You might think it reasonable to say every fornicator or unclean or greedy or shameful person has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. But perhaps shamefulness is in the one only passively defiled in secret, by which, even inflamed, someone checked the impulse toward fornication or toward uncleanness. And in the things above, the things that prevent inheritance—
pass_b_english: —one another," will take it as equal to "forgiving one another," especially because of "as God in Christ forgave us," and will apply it to remission of sins: we must forgive those who sin against us as God forgave us. How did God in Christ forgive our sins? Because the Father, being in Christ, forgave our trespasses? And in Christ he also granted goods—if in Christ there is wisdom he granted us, and truth and righteousness.

[[Ephesians 5:3–4 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:3]] "But fornication and all uncleanness or greed must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints, and shamefulness and foolish talk or coarse jesting, which are not proper, but rather thanksgiving." Origen: Scripture customarily names fellowship with a harlot "fornication." Every sin in the region of fleshly tickling—not only adultery and child-corruption, but whatever else human licentiousness invented in varied frictions—is named uncleanness as a genus.

Greed may be taken simply, or, as elsewhere, as adultery, with "not go beyond and defraud each his brother." Saints must guard against all uncleanness. Shamefulness tracks each kind of licentiousness and is akin to uncleanness: each act in that excretory region shows both the unclean and the shameful. Say this of what is against nature, not of marriage.

What of foolish talk, which must not even be named among saints? Simply, it is buffoonery and laugh-making. Yet those cut off from any wisdom and understanding may also "talk foolishly," and be foolish in their dogmas. Coarse jesting beside it fits the simple reading: ordinary speech uses it for anyone who raises laughter, from foolish talk or any other cause. That too is not proper for saints; rather thanksgiving to God in all things—or "thanksgiving" as when we call people gracious and charming.

So do not be a foolish-talker or coarse jester; be gracious and charming. Because "graciousness" is unusual here, Paul may have used the nearby word and said "thanksgiving." Hebrews may use "thanksgiving" and "thankful" where Greeks say "graciousness" and "gracious." Proverbs' "gracious woman raises a husband's glory" we took as "charming woman"; that would seem forced if Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus did not agree in sense—a woman of grace holding glory.

[[Ephesians 5:5 >> Bible:Ephesians 5:5]] "For this you know: every fornicator or unclean or greedy person—who is an idolater—has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God." Paul forbids six sins, yet ties loss of inheritance to three: fornication, all uncleanness, and greed. If foolish talk and coarse jesting also stripped inheritance, judgment would seem harsh on our weak nature. Those too are improper, yet not so that practicing them alone casts one from Christ's and God's inheritance.

Shamefulness remains. One might add "or shameful" to the inheritance list. Perhaps shamefulness is only the secret passive stain by which someone, even inflamed, checked the drive toward fornication or uncleanness. The things that block inheritance continue in the next unit.
